hints: Think about what happens to the five d orbitals, which are equal in energy in a free ion, when ligands approach to form a complex.
Remember that colour arises when a compound interacts with white light, so consider what energy the d electrons could absorb from visible light.
Link the movement of a d electron between the split energy levels to why only certain wavelengths are removed and a colour is seen.
walkthrough:
Picture the d orbitals splitting**
Start with a free transition metal ion. All five d orbitals have exactly the same energy. When ligands bond around the metal, their lone pairs repel the d electrons unevenly. Some d orbitals point directly at the ligands and are pushed higher in energy, while others point between ligands and stay lower. So you now have a small energy gap between lower and higher d levels.

See light as the energy source for electrons**
That gap happens to match the energy of photons in the visible region. When white light shines on the complex, a d electron can absorb a photon of just the right frequency and jump from the lower set up to the higher set. We call this a d-d transition. Only transition metals with partly filled d orbitals can do this, which is why they are usually coloured.

Connect absorbed light to observed colour**
White light minus the absorbed colour leaves the rest to be transmitted or reflected to your eye. For example, if red light is absorbed to excite the electron, you see the complementary colour, green-blue. Different metals, oxidation states and ligands change the size of the split, so different wavelengths are absorbed and different colours appear.

Final answer: In presence of ligands the d orbitals split into two sets of different energy.
Visible light is absorbed to provide energy to promote an electron from the lower d set to the higher d set.
The colour observed is the complementary colour to that absorbed.

hints: Use the observations to identify the products, the brown gas from concentrated nitric acid and the green-blue solution containing copper(II).
Write the skeleton with $\text{Cu}$ and $\text{HNO}_3$ as reactants and $\text{Cu(NO}_3)_2$, $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ as products, then balance atoms and charge.
walkthrough:
Translate observations into formulae**
Copper metal is oxidised to $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, seen as the green-blue $\text{Cu(NO}_3)_2$ solution. Concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ is reduced to the brown gas $\text{NO}_2$, not $\text{NO}$. Water must also form to balance H and O. So your skeleton is $\text{Cu} + \text{HNO}_3 \rightarrow \text{Cu(NO}_3)_2 + \text{NO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Balance to get the mole ratio**
You need two nitrate ions in $\text{Cu(NO}_3)_2$ plus two more in $2\text{NO}_2$, so you need $4\text{HNO}_3$ in total. That gives $4\text{H}$ which makes $2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Check: $\text{Cu}$ 1 to 1, N 4 to 4, H 4 to 4, O 12 to 12. The balanced equation is $$\text{Cu} + 4\text{HNO}_3 \rightarrow \text{Cu(NO}_3)_2 + 2\text{NO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

hints: Start from the titration data by calculating moles of thiosulfate used, using $n = c \times V$ with volume in $\text{dm}^3$.
Use the two given equations to link moles of $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$ to moles of $\text{I}_2$ and then to moles of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ in the $25.0\,\text{cm}^3$ portion.
Remember the $25.0\,\text{cm}^3$ portion is only one tenth of the $250\,\text{cm}^3$ flask, so scale up to find total moles of copper from the brass.
Convert total moles of copper to mass using $A_r = 63.5$ and then express as a percentage of the $1.75\,\text{g}$ sample.
walkthrough:
Find moles of thiosulfate actually used**
This is a back calculation. The burette reading tells you how much $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$ reacted with the liberated iodine. Convert $\text{cm}^3$ to $\text{dm}^3$ by dividing by 1000: $$n(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}) = c \times V = 0.100 \times \frac{22.40}{1000} = 2.24 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{mol}$$

Work back through the two equations to copper**
Look closely at the stoichiometry: $$\text{I}_2 + 2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-} \rightarrow 2\text{I}^- + \text{S}_4\text{O}_6^{2-}$$ $$2\text{Cu}^{2+} + 4\text{I}^- \rightarrow 2\text{CuI} + \text{I}_2$$ One $\text{I}_2$ needs two $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}$, and one $\text{I}_2$ comes from two $\text{Cu}^{2+}$. So overall $2$ mol thiosulfate corresponds to $2$ mol $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, a 1:1 ratio. Therefore $$n(\text{Cu}^{2+} \text{ in } 25.0\,\text{cm}^3) = 2.24 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{mol}$$

Scale from pipette to whole flask**
You only titrated $25.0\,\text{cm}^3$ out of $250\,\text{cm}^3$, a factor of 10. Multiply up: $$n(\text{Cu}^{2+} \text{ total}) = 2.24 \times 10^{-3} \times \frac{250}{25.0} = 2.24 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{mol}$$ This is also the moles of $\text{Cu}$ metal in the original brass, since each $\text{Cu}$ gave one $\text{Cu}^{2+}$. Convert to mass: $$m(\text{Cu}) = 2.24 \times 10^{-2} \times 63.5 = 1.4224\,\text{g}$$

Express as percentage of brass**
Finally divide by the sample mass and multiply by 100: $$\%\text{Cu} = \frac{1.4224}{1.75} \times 100 = 81.3\%$$ to three significant figures. This makes sense for brass, which is mainly copper with zinc.

Final answer: moles $\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-} = 0.100 \times 22.40/1000 = 2.24 \times 10^{-3}$
moles $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ in $25.0\,\text{cm}^3 = 2.24 \times 10^{-3}$
moles $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ in $250\,\text{cm}^3 = 2.24 \times 10^{-2}$; mass $\text{Cu} = 2.24 \times 10^{-2} \times 63.5 = 1.42\,\text{g}$
% $\text{Cu} = 1.4224/1.75 \times 100 = 81.3\%$ to three significant figures.
